_README: This is a REFERENCE TEMPLATE, not a file LDO reads. A workflow has no filesystem access, so config reaches it only via args.config at invocation. Two ways to use this: (1) copy the values into your project's CLAUDE.md so Claude passes them on every run — /ldo-init writes that block for you; (2) pass them inline: Workflow({name:'ldo', args:{task:'...', config:{...}}}). Model names mean whatever your setup routes them to.
_models_note: planner is 'opus' in every tier on purpose — complexity is the Planner's own output, so it structurally can't gate its own model (only the 'medium' row's planner value is ever read at runtime). reviewer is 'opus' in trivial/medium and 'fable' in complex, falling back to 'sonnet' when fable isn't on the proxy route: catching what the coder missed is the whole point of review, and complex work has the most to miss. coder is the role that scales with the tier — haiku/sonnet/opus. reviewerFix routes review rounds 2+ and is set to the same model as reviewer in every tier, so the defaults change nothing — see _reviewerFix_note before lowering it. An override is merged per ROLE, not per tier: setting only {"medium": {"coder": "haiku"}} leaves the other six medium roles at their defaults. An unrecognised tier, role or non-string model name is warned about in the run log and ignored, never passed to the harness.
_reviewerFix_note: Round 1 is an open-ended search for defects nobody has named yet and earns the strongest model. A fix pass is a different, easier job: bounded verification of a list the previous round already wrote down. That argues for a cheaper reviewerFix — but it is a real trade, not a free saving: in a measured run, round 4 found a genuine new major that rounds 1-3 had missed. So the default is deliberately identical to reviewer, and setting reviewerFix lower is how you buy cheaper fix rounds knowing what they can cost. The post-plan log line names both models, so you can check an override took effect.
_planner_note: maxStepsPerRun is a SOFT threshold reported to the Planner, never enforced by the orchestrator — nothing is truncated, blocked, or refused above it. It tells the Planner what this project considers one run's worth of work, and above it the Planner is expected to rate fits_one_run: false unless the steps are genuinely one unit of work. preferSplit: false means 'plan it as one piece', so the Planner only flags a split when the task is incoherent as one run. Both values are interpolated into the Planner's prompt, so changing them reaches the agent doing the rating. The resulting sizing block is advisory — reported to you, never a gate.
_tests_note: A single run used to execute the full test suite 5-8 times: the Coder's baseline, its per-step runs and its end-of-pass run, the Reviewer's own run, and the two runs the revert-and-rerun proof needs to watch one test flip — all repeated on every fix round. scope 'scoped' (the default) narrows the intermediate runs to the files actually touched, using the test_command_scoped template the Planner supplies; scope 'full' restores the old behaviour exactly. What scoped runs cannot catch is a regression in a module this change never touched — that is what the one full run is for, and why the default pairs scoped with fullSuiteAt 'final-pass'. Scoping only happens when the Planner supplied a template that survives validation (one {paths} placeholder, no shell metacharacters, a recognised runner); anything else, and every resumed plan, falls back to the full suite unchanged. fullSuiteAt 'never' means the full suite runs NOWHERE in the pipeline and you own that gate: on 'never' and 'ship' the Coder and the Reviewer are each handed an explicit do-not-run block on every pass, so the setting removes the run rather than labelling the result afterwards. It only applies under scope 'scoped' — with scope 'full' the baseline and every per-step run are already the whole suite, so there is nothing to defer, and the setting is neutralised with a log line instead of reporting 'disabled' for a run that tested everything. Whatever the setting, the run's result carries full_suite_status (ran | not_run | disabled | deferred_to_ship), and any value but 'ran' appends a FULL SUITE NOT RUN line to the verdict summary — it annotates, it never blocks, so read it before treating approved: true as a merge signal.
_backlog_note: Where the Record phase puts backlog items. The default is 'file' — docs/BACKLOG.md, or docs/backlog/<label>.md in a parallel or isolate:true run — and GitHub is opt-in, which is the inverse of how this used to work. The reason is not preference: the host safety classifier refuses the ATTEMPT at external publication, not its result, so a Recorder that runs even one `gh` probe is ended before it writes anything, and the review report and architecture doc go with it — three runs in one session ended that way with record_status: failed and no artifact at all. On 'file' the Recorder is therefore told not to run `gh` at all, not even to check whether it is available; 'try and fall back' is the failure, not the safety net. Setting 'github' opts in: one issue per backlog item, labelled `backlog` only if that label already exists, and if `gh` turns out to be missing, unauthenticated or refused, the Recorder falls back to the file and says so in its notes. An unrecognised value warns and keeps 'file'.
_design_note: LDO does not own your design documents — it defines no format, ships no template and writes none of them; see README, "What LDO does not own". This is the one thing it does own: a mapping from a path glob to a document of yours that describes that code, so a run whose files_changed matched the glob while the document stayed untouched is reported. Issue #20 measured 4 of 46 design files untouched for six weeks while their code moved, and detecting that needs no format at all — just the glob, the path and the files the run already reported. It costs no filesystem access: the match is pure string comparison over data the orchestrator is holding anyway. The result is a BACKLOG ITEM, never a write — the Recorder is told explicitly never to open, create or edit a document named here, and the orchestrator logs a warning if it reports doing so anyway. `glob` supports `**` (crosses directories) and `*` (does not); every other character is literal, so `src/(a|b)/**` is not an alternation, and nothing is compiled to a regular expression. Each changed file is compared in its repo-relative form, so a path reported from inside a worktree still matches, and the glob may match the tail of a longer path — `docs` also matches `vendor/docs`, which over-reports a backlog line rather than staying silent. `doc` must be a repo-relative path with no `..` and no dot- or dash-leading segment: it is rendered into an agent's prompt as a path. Up to 40 entries; an entry whose glob is over 200 characters or carries more than 10 wildcards is rejected with a warning. Omit the block entirely and nothing changes — no map, no prompt block, byte-identical Record prompt.
_stallMs_note: Claude Code's stall watchdog counts only tool calls as progress, so an agent composing a large structured output (a long plan, a full verdict) looks identical to a hung one until it's already aborted. Keyed by role, not tier, because output size tracks the schema the role fills, not task complexity. recorder sits at the 180000 harness default on purpose — it writes through tools, so tool_use events keep resetting its clock naturally. Values are MILLISECONDS with a floor of 1000: a seconds/ms mix-up like 480 would abort the role instantly six times in a row, so it's rejected with a warning rather than passed through.

_phases._comment: Plan, Code, and Review always run. Two are conditional.
_phases.security: runs when the Planner rates security_surface 'elevated'; force with security: true/false or securityByDefault

_securityByDefault: Not set here on purpose. Omit the key and the Planner decides (Security runs when it rates the surface 'elevated'). Add "securityByDefault": true to always threat-model, or false to never — either value overrides the Planner.
